extracted.intended_audience: economists, legal scholars, policymakers, and practitioners interested in patent law, patent policy, and the economics of innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing patent quality, litigation outcomes, and reform options in the U.S. patent system, focusing on uncertainty, examination, incentives to challenge patents, and antitrust implications of settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty and nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO tests for novelty by looking for prior art and grants a patent only if the invention would not have been obvious 'to a person of ordinary skill in the art' at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must disclose relevant prior art of which they are aware; the PTO looks to patents, publications, and existing products to assess novelty and obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope of a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a patent is defined by its 'claims.' Examiners evaluate whether the invention described in the claims meets statutory patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim drafting determines exclusionary reach; examination focuses on the claims rather than broader specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure / enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application disclosure must be sufficient so that those skilled in the art can make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate disclosure is necessary to justify the grant of exclusive rights; insufficiency can be a basis for invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for invalidity (presumption of validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current U.S. law, issued patents enjoy a presumption of validity; to invalidate a patent requires 'clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals exist to lower this to a 'preponderance of the evidence' standard to better reflect uncertainty and reduce improperly issued patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental dimensions of patent uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty about (1) the commercial significance of the invention being patented and (2) the validity and scope of the legal right being granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two forms of uncertainty shape appropriate reform choices: examination reforms address commercial-significance uncertainty; litigation/opposition reforms address validity/scope uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO examination resource allocation (focus on commercially significant applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many patents are of little commercial significance, it may be inefficient to expend the same examination resources across all applications; resources should be focused on applications likely to be commercially important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable correlates of value (e.g., number of claims, number of prior art references, time invested in prosecution) to triage; concentrate examiner attention on new/rapidly changing technology areas (software, business methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant prior-art disclosure obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are required to disclose relevant prior art of which they are aware but are not required to conduct a thorough prior-art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One reform proposal is to require applicants to conduct a full prior-art search to reduce information asymmetry between applicants and the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation practice and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. applicants can file continuation applications repeatedly, with no limit, enabling patentees to pursue broader claims over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuations allow strategic hedging but also encourage applicants to file early and then seek broader scope later; reform proposals include limiting continuation practice to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance fees and lapse as signals of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents require maintenance fees (at years 3, 7, and 11) and a large share lapse for failure to pay, indicating many patents are of little value to owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High lapse rates (55–67%) signal skewed value distribution; maintenance fees act as a market test of private value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent value distribution and predictors of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Value of patents is highly skewed (top 1% far more valuable than median); observable predictors include industry, number of prior art references, number of claims, and time invested in prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These predictors can inform examiner triage and selection of applications for deeper review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent thickets and portfolio density
rubrics_metrics.description: In some industries, numerous related patents can apply to a single product, producing patent 'thickets' that complicate design-arounds and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thickets can create royalty-stacking and raise entry costs; cross-licensing and patent pools can ameliorate but may disadvantage new entrants without portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party opposition / reexamination procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An opposition system (as in Europe) allows third parties to challenge issued patents administratively; U.S. inter partes reexamination exists but has been rarely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions can be effective in identifying weak patents, but any system relying on third-party challenges faces free-riding incentives that under-supply challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selection of patent strength (Standard vs Super Patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to allow applicants to select between a normal examination leading to a Standard Patent or a more rigorous process leading to a Super Patent, with courts giving different weight to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-selection avoids requiring the PTO to perfectly predict commercial significance; courts would need to accord different presumptions of validity accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising nonobviousness standard as reform
rubrics_metrics.description: One reform option is to raise the legal standard for nonobviousness to make it harder to obtain patents for marginal improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher standards could reduce issuance of low-quality patents but risk denying true innovations; trade-offs must be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional incentives for examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural problems at the PTO (high examiner turnover and incentives that reward allowances over rejections) encourage issuance of patents of doubtful quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms include hiring/retention improvements and altering incentive systems to encourage more careful rejections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation-stage uncertainty and grounds for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: When litigated, patents face substantial uncertainty—common invalidity grounds include prior art-based obviousness/novelty and statutory bars; claim construction and doctrines like equivalents and inequitable conduct also create uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately half of litigated patents are found invalid; claim-construction variability and doctrines like inequitable conduct complicate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents and scope expansion limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents can permit patentees to expand a patent's reach beyond literal claim language; courts have been moving to place limits on this doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the doctrine reduces post-grant expansion of scope and litigation uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct as a source of unenforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be rendered unenforceable if the patentee deceived or omitted information to the PTO; allegations of inequitable conduct are common and described as widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though relatively few patents are ultimately held unenforceable for inequitable conduct, the prevalence of such claims generates litigation complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement doctrine and enhanced damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful infringement permits treble damages where an infringer knowingly infringes a valid patent; current rules are complex and may require attorney opinions to avoid willfulness findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals include eliminating or modifying willfulness doctrine to reflect real uncertainty in patent scope and validity or to place it on a more objective footing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction standard in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions may be granted if the patentee is likely to prevail and would suffer irreparable harm; courts deny injunctions if serious questions exist about validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In certain contexts (e.g., pharmaceuticals), statutory preliminary injunction regimes (e.g., 30-month automatic stays) affect settlement incentives and reverse payment analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent settlements and antitrust test (consumer surplus comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shapiro's proposed framework: a settlement cannot lead to lower expected consumer surplus than would arise from ongoing litigation; settlements that reduce expected consumer surplus are presumptively anticompetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application typically requires assessment of patent strength; presence of substantial reverse payments from patentee to accused infringer may indicate anticompetitive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse payments (pay-for-delay) scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments from patent holders to alleged infringers to stay off the market (reverse payments) can extend exclusion beyond what the patent grant would allow and may be presumptively anticompetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large reverse payments are inconsistent with a patentee's claim of strong patent; courts and the FTC have scrutinized such agreements in the pharmaceutical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private incentives to challenge patents (public-good and pass-through problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges are undersupplied because invalidation is a public good (benefits diffuse consumers/competitors) and royalty costs are passed through to customers, muting challengers' incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why weak patents may command royalties and why reliance on private litigation to police PTO errors is inadequate; policy responses could provide rewards for successful challenges or lower litigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and time of PTO examination (capacity constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average examination takes nearly three years but examiners spend only about 18 hours per application on average; PTO backlog and limited examiner time contribute to issuance of many doubtful patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity constraints justify targeted resource allocation rather than across-the-board deeper examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-examination and binding effect issues
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. inter partes re-examination and re-examination with third-party participation have been permitted since 1999 but are rarely used; outcomes of opposition/reexamination may be binding in subsequent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding administrative outcomes can deter use of opposition processes; making oppositions attractive and effective requires careful design to avoid disincentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of reforms to account for asymmetric information
rubrics_metrics.description: Any patent reform must account for superior applicant information about commercial significance and prior art; reforms that ignore information asymmetries may be ineffective or counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms that elicit applicant information or align incentives (e.g., fee structures, self-selection of patent strength, opposition procedures) are preferable to blunt across-the-board measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus examination on technology areas with hard-to-identify prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners might concentrate resources in fields where prior art is difficult to find (e.g., software, business methods) because these areas are more likely to yield improperly issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted focus risks applicants steering filings away from targeted fields; policy design must anticipate strategic applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic modeling of probabilistic patents and royalty setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Model patents as probabilistic rights (right to try to exclude) rather than absolute rights; this affects optimal royalties/licensing and the social cost of uncertain patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilistic treatment yields insights into why even weak patents can extract large royalties and why settlements/license terms may not reflect true patent strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of observable prosecution features to predict patent value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable features—industry, number of prior-art references, number of claims, and time invested in prosecution—are significant predictors of ultimate patent value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work suggests PTO could triage applications using such signals to allocate examination effort more effectively.
